windows.label: Human
windows.text: Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don’t think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes the truth is that you were abused, coerced, or seriously deceived. So how much you say, and to whom, and how publicly, really depends on what happened and why you’re telling people.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Once you’re out, you can see things you genuinely couldn’t see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed. And don’t turn your ex into a cartoon villain: try to understand whatever was true in their perspective too, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Sometimes the easiest story is that they were fake all along, because it explains everything. Grab it only if it really is the simplest explanation of what happened. People who aren’t heavily invested in seeing your innocence can help you tell, and a therapist, pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.
Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don’t use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex’s wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don’t use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him: looking honestly at your part doesn’t erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, “What would Mr. Rogers do?” (if you’re old enough to remember that show).
I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. It can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You’re not a yo-yo.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Once I’m attached, “I’m taking a chance on her” starts turning into “she’s the right person” after we’ve been together for a while.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something, and sometimes nothing changed except that now I’m attached, so the new certainty is just harder for me to question.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
If I have sex with somebody quickly, that’s a reason not to move in quickly too, and to keep seeing friends, have some kind of community around the relationship, and pick actual dates to ask how it’s going. Moving in together right away is basically getting into a common-law marriage without discussing it, and it’s too easy for me to assume the relationship is going well just because we’re already entangled.
I can know I want her much faster than I can know whether I want to raise children with her, live in community with her, or build a life with her.
At some point one of you will ask, “Why am I special to you? Why are you with me and not somebody else?” If the answer is basically, “We had sex and got hitched?” I don’t know, that’s a damn shame.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
For me, the window of objectivity starts closing abruptly once it seems like sex will definitely be happening soon and I’m flowing with that timeline. I begin idealizing her more, and after sex I may suddenly feel unable to leave because maybe she’s pregnant, etc.
Maybe I’m not representative of the modern degen dating scene. If you’re quite numb and used to casual sex, perhaps the window closes later, or even never. But for me, this is the pattern, and it seems like it would be healthy in a healthy, natural, small society.
The attachment theory part comes from my own experience and from reading I’ve done. Sex turns on bonding chemistry—oxytocin, dopamine, vasopressin—that usually biases us toward attachment.
People call oxytocin the “love hormone,” as if getting more attached should make you feel closer and safer. If closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home, but if it came with neglect, abuse, or if people disappeared on you, you can get more attached and more freaked out at the same time.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: You might get anxious or suspicious.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
You might feel worthless or fight or flight mode may kick in.
There are several main types of brain chemistries that people have, and they determine part of what attracts us, according to Helen Fisher’s research:

windows.label: Human
windows.text: It can go either way, but often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. Refusing to name the relationship doesn’t make the responsibility disappear. What they don’t escape is the existential void created by another superficial fix. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.
A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: I see the good.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.
I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes?

windows.label: Human
windows.text: What’s the pattern?

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this?

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That’s my question.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.
My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem: a lot of women have seen me that way.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.
She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, there was the forest-and-mansion line I mentioned earlier that made it feel unconditional. Best drug I ever had.
I don’t know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.
So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That wasn’t the whole story.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.
Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her, and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.
That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Going slowly can show you how somebody’s moods move over time, how they treat you, and how they treat other people, but it still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.

windows.label: AI-Generated
windows.text:
You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there, touch or smell feels wrong, your desire levels or kinks don’t fit, one person is sexually shut down, or the bodies just don’t connect.
Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Sometimes bad sexual fit still feels like, “Let’s just be friends!”
Saying, “The sex isn’t working for me,” may sound like, “I only love you if the sex is good.” But universal love doesn’t make someone special.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: It isn’t romance.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
It’s the basis of any good relationship of any kind.
I can still love her and not want to be in a romantic relationship with her. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or we’re friends who care deeply about each other.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.
A peer can give another angle.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That’s why I recommend peer counseling outside the couple.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
If my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don’t understand it.
I also have to deal with what happens in my body.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: My mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Meanwhile my body feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow. It becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
That is another reason to have a peer counselor.
Crying also contains a type of automatic erratic breathwork. Breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Reduced breathing or the Buteyko method is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that, and other times it’s hard to tell. I explain more of the body-based options in my Somatic Modalities guide.
Meditation is also helpful. For most people, I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first or make them primary meditation targets. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet. Meditation without grounding in those approaches can easily be a road into spiritual bypassing.
